title: Asha and Tumble's Water Walk
markdown:
Asha helped at the quiet little museum, where the stone walls held the day’s warmth long after the visitors had gone. She liked small wonders: dust in a sunbeam, the tick of the clock in the natural-history hall, the way Tumble the goat treated every courtyard as if it had been planted for him personally.

This evening Tumble stood at the garden pond and gave a low bleat, more sigh than complaint. His fluffy tail drooped. Across the water, a patch of clover shone green and sweet, beaded with the last of the day’s dew.

“I know,” Asha said, her palm on his warm grey wool. “Your favourite. And the long way round is a very long way when you are hungry.”

Tumble had already tried. He had stretched his neck until his ears flopped. He had dipped a hoof into the shimmering water; it was too deep to wade, and he was not a strong swimmer. He had sploshed back onto the bank, the clover-scent close and useless.

Asha did not hurry him. She sat on her heels at the water’s edge and watched. The pond held the twilight like a polished tray. A cloud snagged on the museum roof and tore itself slowly into blue.

Then a flicker: a creature no bigger than her thumbnail, iridescent, dancing across the surface. It was not swimming. Its many delicate legs barely seemed to touch. No ripples worth the name. Only a whisper of disturbance.

“Look, Tumble. A tiny dancer.”

Tumble’s ears perked, a hopeful twitch. The water-strider skittered and hopped. Asha leaned closer. The water curved gently around each leg, as if the surface were a soft strong sheet, resilient and giving.

“The water has a skin,” she breathed.

Tumble, who believed in trying, set one hoof on that skin. It broke. The hoof sank with a small honest gulp. Asha took his collar and drew him back, her mouth dry with almost-laughter.

“You are not thumbnail-sized. That is not an insult. It is physics.”

She tested what they had. A pebble dropped: it vanished. A dry pine needle, laid as carefully as a letter, rested. The water dimpled under it and did not quite let go. Tumble watched, brown eyes like moonlit pools, and then looked again at the far clover, still a faraway dream.

Professor Imani had been on the nearby bench the whole time, a quiet fact of the garden. She did not interrupt the pine needle.

Asha found a sheet of birch bark among the museum’s kindling, light as a dry leaf and almost as wide as Tumble’s head. She slid it onto the pond. It sat. She laid a second needle on it to be sure. Then, from a fallen log that reached a little way out, she used a long stick to nudge a drifting spray of clover — blossoms that had already fallen onto the water and were sitting there like tiny boats — onto the bark. The water’s skin helped. When she pulled too hard, a bloom ducked under and was lost. When she was as careful as the strider, the bark came home with green cargo.

Tumble munched, a melody of crunch and relief. Asha ferried two more small loads. It was not the whole far patch. It was enough for evening.

“Asha,” Professor Imani said, voice like rustling leaves, “do you know what you have been using?”

Asha looked from the still-busy strider to the pond’s calm. “Surface tension. The water’s skin. Strong enough for something light, if you do not punch through it.”

Imani’s smile was the kind that did not need to prove itself. “Precisely. Weight spread out. Legs like threads. A needle. A scrap of bark. It is why so many small creatures can dance there. Tumble would need to be a much more surprising goat.”

Tumble, his belly somewhat filled, sighed the satisfied sigh of someone who had been taken seriously. He looked at the pond, no longer only a barrier. Asha sat with him while the sky went from blue to the colour of old pewter, and did not mention the long path around the reeds. They could walk it tomorrow, when hunger was not doing all the talking.

The water held the first star. Asha wondered what else might rest on that skin if she asked it politely enough — a paperclip, a leaf-boat, a question. Tumble leaned his head against her knee, and the museum clock ticked, unhurried, as if evening had all the time in the world.
characters: Asha (a museum helper), Tumble (a goat), Imani (a professor)
author: StoryGen Community
